articles.title: German boat dealer suspected of supplying Channel smuggling gangs, BBC finds
articles.snippet: Nearly a third of crossings in early 2026 allegedly involved boats or engines from the German man's firm.
articles.full_text:
German boat dealer suspected of supplying Channel smuggling gangs, BBC finds
- Published
A German boat dealer is suspected by European authorities of being a key supplier to migrant smugglers operating in the English Channel, the BBC can reveal.
Nearly a third of small-boat crossings in the first four months of this year allegedly involved boats or engines from MaReBoote, a small firm in western Germany, according to files we have seen.
The managing director, Marvin Reuter, is contesting extradition to France, where he could face smuggling, criminal conspiracy and involuntary manslaughter charges.
His equipment is suspected of being linked to two fatal accidents, in which four men died.
We confronted the 35-year-old at his business near Dortmund, but he would not answer our questions. He said he was reporting us to the police.
Reuter cannot be formally charged until extradited to France but could face jail time, if tried and convicted. He is presumed innocent until proven guilty.
The BBC - alongside German broadcasters WDR and NDR, newspaper SÃ¼ddeutsche Zeitung (SZ) - and France's Le Monde newspaper - has obtained and reviewed hundreds of police, court and tax documents about the case. We have blurred images of Reuter because of German privacy rules.
Investigators, we have learned, believe they have uncovered clear, persistent links between Reuter and smuggling networks.
Evidence has been gathered through the confessions of alleged accomplices and covert jail-cell recordings of an alleged gang chief - as well as the two deadly crossing attempts.
At least 82 boats from Reuter's firm reached the English coast in just over two years to May, according to French investigations.
There are also press photos dating back five years showing the MaReBoote logo on dinghies crowded with migrants.
In 2021, Reuter told the Sun and Guardian he felt "frustrated" and "anxious" that his vessels had ended up in the hands of smugglers.
There was no suggestion, at that time, that authorities suspected him of wrongdoing as a German detective reportedly told the Sun: "This would be like if somebody buys a Mercedes and does something in another country which is wrong. The Mercedes seller can't help that."
It is not exactly clear when police suspicions were aroused.
French prosecutor Samuel Finielz would not comment on the details of the investigation but confirmed the head of a German company is currently the subject of a European Arrest Warrant.
The warrant was issued in May this year and relates to alleged offences dating back to December 2024.
While selling boats is "perfectly legal" it becomes illegal, said Finielz, "when one is fully aware that they will be used by networks involved in illegal immigration or human trafficking".
Case files we have seen say that German police had learned from UK authorities that 29% of detected crossings this year, up to the end of April, involved boats and/or engines linked to MaReBoote.
In France, five other men have already been charged as part of the investigation - an Iranian, three Iraqis and a Syrian.
In one of the two fatal incidents where Reuter's equipment is suspected to be involved, one of those who died was also Syrian.
Suliman al Husein would have just turned 20 when he died, according to a birth date listed in the files.
News reports at the time say he suffered a cardiac arrest after likely being crushed on a packed dinghy during a failed launch, west of Calais, in January 2025.
He was the first migrant to die in the English Channel that year. His body was found on the floor of the boat which, investigators allege, bore the MaReBoote logo.
The case against Reuter also stems from a chance arrest when French police pulled over a vehicle with German plates, near the northern port city of Boulogne-sur-Mer.
The BMW, which was towing a trailer, was spotted overtaking another vehicle at speed in the early hours of a morning in May this year - police records say.
Inside the car were two German nationals who - according to a subsequent search - were transporting jerry cans of fuel, a boat engine, pumps and a rolled up inflatable dinghy.
The men claimed they had been paid up to â¬1,000-a-time (Â£830) to make several, similar drops to "foreigners" on the coast, interrogation records show.
"Of course I knew that it wasn't legal," one is said to have admitted under questioning. "The money made me turn a blind eye."

Both men, who have since been convicted for smuggling offences, allegedly implicated Marvin Reuter as the man who had hired and paid them for this work.
Police files say both the BMW and the boat it was carrying had MaReBoote logos on them.
Marvin Reuter was arrested in Germany in May and later released, pending extradition.
On the day of his arrest, German police also seized more than 30 dinghies and 9,000 life jackets. Equipment which, we can now reveal, was allegedly linked to Reuter.
The BBC was previously granted access to see this haul, held in a police warehouse at a secret location in western Germany.
Meanwhile, further evidence has been gleaned from the bugging of a jail cell of a suspected gang chief, who is being held in pre-trial detention in France.
Recordings captured the inmate talking about buying nautical equipment from a German firm run by a man with Reuter's first name: Marvin - according to files we have seen.
The MaReBoote company address was also discovered on the alleged smuggler's phone, the case files say.
When we confronted Reuter last month at his business in the town of Werne, in the state of North Rhine-Westphalia, he told us to leave and drove off.
He then returned a short time later and said he was reporting us to the police. He did not answer our questions.
We approached him in writing before and after this encounter including a detailed request for comment. In response to that request, he did not address the specific allegations but accused us of harassment.
It is understood Reuter's lawyers have challenged his extradition, citing overcrowding in French prisons as one reason. Their client should face any allegations in Germany, they argue.
In Germany, it became explicitly illegal to aid smuggling to the UK at the end of last year after a prior BBC investigation exposed the country's role as a storage hub for gangs. Before then, some anti-smuggling laws in Germany had no longer applied to the UK because of Brexit.
The raid that saw the seizure of equipment that was allegedly linked to Reuter marked the first time the new law had been used.
Small boat crossings have dropped significantly in 2026, with British authorities citing law enforcement as a "key factor". However, illegal migration into Europe has also been falling.
The UK National Crime Agency's (NCA) deputy director for organized immigration crime, Dan Cannatella-Barcroft, praised Germany's "commitment" to tackling people-smuggling but acknowledged the country would remain "an important piece of the puzzle".
While a gap in the law has been closed, Germany's proximity to France, wider transport links and the fact that some of the Kurdish-dominated gangs are based there, means it is expected to stay as a transit point in the illegal small-boats trade.
The "vast majority" of small boats equipment in the past few years has come through Germany, Cannatella-Barcroft told the BBC - much of it made in China and having been routed through Turkey.

articles.title: Diesel tanker carrying up to 7,000 tonnes capsizes near Ibiza, killing one
articles.snippet: The possible environmental damage is still being assessed by Spain's sea rescue service.
articles.full_text:
Diesel tanker carrying up to 7,000 tonnes capsizes near Ibiza, killing one
- Published
An oil tanker carrying up to 7,000 tonnes of diesel has capsized off the coast of Ibiza, leaving one crew member dead, authorities have said.
The Med Emre, a Malta-flagged vessel, was carrying 17 crew members who were all rescued. However seven were taken to hospital and one was later pronounced dead, Balearic Islands emergency services confirmed.
The six crew receiving treatment reportedly suffered minor injuries, such as hypothermia, Spanish media reports.
The possible environmental damage is being assessed by a plane and Spain's pollution control vessel, Clara Campoamor, which is owned by the country's national maritime rescue service.
"There is still little information available about a possible fuel spill," Balearic Islands' President Marga Prohens wrote on X.
Regional emergencies director Pablo GÃ¡rriz said the tanker had not completely sunk, as had been originally reported. The vessel remains, however, partially submerged.
That made conditions more favourable for carrying out recovery operations, he said, "as we have gone from the possibility of the vessel being at a depth of 1,000m to a situation that allows operations to be carried out on the surface".
The Med Emre capsized 25 nautical miles (46 km; 29 miles) from Ibiza's coastline and 57 nautical miles from Valencia. It is unclear what caused the sinking.
The chemical tanker was en route from Algeciras, in southern Spain, to Barcelona in the north-east.
Rescuers in Valencia received a distress call around 22:30 local time (21:30 GMT) on Wednesday, according to Spanish media. Minutes later, the vessel reported a leak and the crew said it was leaning at a 90-degree angle.
The injured crew members have been taken to hospitals in Valencia and Can Misses Hospital in Ibiza, President Prohens said.
Ibiza's marine environment was added to the Unesco World Heritage List in 1999. In particular, it is home to dense prairies of Posidonia oceanic seagrass, which is found only in the Mediterranean basin and plays a vital role in supporting local marine biodiversity.
In 2002, Spain experienced one of its worst environmental disasters when the Prestige oil tanker ran into trouble off Galicia's coastline. It spilled more than 60,000 tonnes of heavy fuel oil into the sea.

articles.title: Gérard Depardieu to stand trial for alleged rape of actress in 2018, court rules
articles.snippet: A Paris appeals court rules Depardieu will go on trial for the alleged rape of Charlotte Arnould.
articles.full_text:
GÃ©rard Depardieu to stand trial for alleged rape of actress in 2018, court rules
- Published
French film actor GÃ©rard Depardieu is to stand trial for the alleged rape of actress Charlotte Arnould, a Paris appeals court has confirmed.
Arnould, who was 22 at the time, had reported the alleged rape several days after going to his house in Paris to rehearse a play.
She has waived her right to anonymity and her lawyer said Thursday's ruling was a "first" and the forthcoming trial would be historic.
Depardieu, 77, had contested his indictment on two counts of rape. In a letter published in Le Figaro in 2023, Depardieu strongly denied Arnould's allegations, saying "there was never any coercion or violence between us".
Depardieu was for decades a leading figure in French and international cinema for roles in Green Card, The Man in the Iron Mask and the Asterix films. He was awarded France's LÃ©gion d'honneur in 1996.
But in recent years a series of allegations have been made against him over his conduct on film sets and elsewhere in the wake of France's #MeToo movement, known as balance ton porc (call out your pig).
Last year, he was given an 18-month suspended jail term after he was found guilty of sexually assaulting two women on a film set in Paris in May. He was also placed on the sex offenders register and ordered to pay compensation.
He dropped his appeal against the ruling last week and offered "sincere apologies" for his behaviour on the set of director Jean Becker's 2021 film Les Volets Verts (The Green Shutters).
Depardieu had been a friend of Charlotte Arnould's father and on 7 August 2018 she had gone to his home, where much of what happened was captured on the actor's own CCTV.
Arnould's case was initially dismissed for insufficient evidence, but after she filed a civil complaint, a judicial investigation was opened in the summer of 2020.
Speaking outside the Paris appeal court on Thursday, her lawyer Carine Durrieu Diebolt said the ruling was a victory for her client for whom it was "genuinely a relief".
The appeal court said that while Depardieu should stand trial for what took place on that day, he would not be tried for a further alleged rape at a hotel six days later.
Depardieu's lawyer David-Olivier Kaminski told reporters that court had partly ruled in his favour: "As soon as we get the ruling, we will look into the possibility of appealing to the Court of Cassation."
Meanwhile, Depardieu is under a separate investigation alongside French author Michel Houellebecq for "allegations of a sexual nature".
French authorities confirmed their inquiry last week, following reports of an alleged "gang rape" on the set of the film Thalasso in 2018.

articles.title: Pregnant US inmate escapes in prison vehicle after medical appointment
articles.snippet: Rebecca Taylor had been imprisoned in New Mexico for multiple theft and burglary charges.
articles.full_text:
Pregnant US inmate escapes in prison vehicle after medical appointment
- Published
A pregnant inmate has escaped from custody in the US state of New Mexico, after taking control of a police vehicle while returning to prison from a prenatal appointment, the state's corrections department has said.
Rebecca Taylor, 26, took control of the Dodge Journey and drove away when the team transporting her and another inmate stopped to pick up food in Albuquerque, local media reported.
The New Mexico Corrections Department said that the vehicle and her prison jumpsuit were later recovered, but Taylor remains on the run.
She had been imprisoned for multiple theft and burglary charges, the department said in a Facebook statement.
Local media reported that another inmate, also travelling back from a prenatal appointment, was able to get out of the car as Taylor took control on Wednesday morning.
The corrections department has said that a multi-agency search for Taylor is under way. The BBC has approached it for an update.
The Albuquerque Journal reported that Taylor is currently in her second trimester of pregnancy. For this reason, she was not restrained during transportation, department spokesperson Brittany Roembach said.
"It is the understanding right now that one officer was with the vehicle but not inside of the vehicle when this occurred," she was quoted as saying.
All prisons in New Mexico went into lockdown following Taylor's escape, but it was lifted at 06:00 on Thursday.
However the prison where she was being held, the Western New Mexico Corrections Facility, will remain on "modified movement", and no visitors are currently allowed.
The public has been told not to approach Rebecca Taylor if they see her, and call police straight away.

articles.title: Two Italians killed in strike in Kuwait, as Iran denies responsibility
articles.snippet: The pair were technicians for German company Rheinmetall, according to Italy's foreign ministry.
articles.full_text:
Two Italians killed in strike in Kuwait, as Iran denies responsibility
- Published
Two Italian nationals have died following a strike on a facility in Kuwait which both countries have blamed on Iran.
The pair were technicians working for German arms manufacturing company Rheinmetall, Italy's foreign ministry said.
Iran has denied responsibility for the attack, with armed forces spokesperson Abolfazl Shekarchi saying "no military or offensive operations have been conducted" by its military.
Kuwait's defence ministry said earlier that four people - the two Italians, a Kuwaiti national and Pakistani national - had been injured from falling shrapnel after a number of drones from Iran were detected and intercepted.
It comes just over a week after Kuwait said it had repelled overnight Iranian drone attacks on an airbase which hosts US forces - the first strikes in more than two months on the country.
Recent exchanges of fire between the US and Iran, and a deadlock in negotiations, have raised fears of a major escalation in the war.
The conflict began when US and Israel attacked Iran in late February, with Iran retaliating by launching missiles and drones at Israel and Gulf Arab states hosting US military assets and personnel.
Iranian-backed militias in the region have also carried out attacks on the US's Gulf allies.
Kuwait's Army said the latest attack was on a "vital site in the country" and was the result of "heinous Iranian aggression", while confirming the deaths of the two Italian nationals.
Meanwhile, Italy's foreign ministry said in a statement: "An explosion caused by a drone attack... occurred at a site where two Italian technicians from the company Rheinmetall Italia were working."
The two Italian nationals were working at an air defence detection station and performing maintenance work on systems used by the Kuwaiti Armed Forces, according to Italian press agency Ansa, citing Italy's foreign ministry.
Italian media outlets have named the two individuals. One of the men was reported to be 36, while the other was 65 and nearing retirement.
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni wrote on X: "On my own behalf and on behalf of the government, I express my deepest sympathy and offer my heartfelt condolences to the victims' families.
"My thoughts are with all those affected by the attack and their families."
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen wrote on social media: "We must step up pressure on Iran to end these unacceptable attacks against its neighbours and our partners in the Gulf.
"Today's events are a further reminder that security in the Gulf is a security issue for us all."

articles.title: Egyptian authorities arrest motorist over tanker crash that killed 31
articles.snippet: Officials say the man confessed to travelling at speed and clipping the fuel truck as he was overtaking traffic.
articles.full_text:
Egyptian authorities arrest motorist over tanker crash that killed 31
- Published
Egyptian authorities have arrested a man accused of causing a tanker crash and massive fire that killed 31 people on a busy Cairo highway.
The public prosecutor's office said the motorist had confessed to driving at 110km/h (68mph) along a section of ring road, to the north of the old city centre, and clipping the tanker with the side of his car as he changed lanes.
Sources close to the investigation were earlier quoted by state media as saying a high-voltage cable had fallen in front of the fuel truck, causing the driver to lose control.
Twenty-one others were injured in the crash in the Warraq neighbourhood on Wednesday evening, with hospitals treating patients for burns and smoke inhalation.
The public prosecutor's office said on Thursday that "upon questioning the suspect and confronting him with the findings of the investigation... he confessed to committing the act".
"He added that, while moving between traffic lanes and overtaking vehicles, the left side of his car collided with the right rear side of the tanker. This caused him to lose control of the steering wheel and his car veered to the far right of the road."
At the same time, one of the fuel tanker's tyres burst, causing it to veer into the highway's central reservation, hit the concrete barrier and overturn, spilling fuel and igniting a fire, the prosecutor's office said.
Egyptian authorities have not named the suspect accused of causing the fatal crash, but they said he had been travelling with his father at the time.
The raised motorway - a major artery for traffic around the Egyptian capital - was reopened by emergency services hours after the crash occurred, with the burnt-out wrecks of cars shifted to the side by bulldozers and diggers.
A cabinet minister said on Thursday that 10 million Egyptian pounds (Â£139,000; $182,000) had been donated to the families of the victims, while the nation's sports minister said all state-run celebratory activities would be cancelled in the aftermath of the crash.
Egypt has suffered several deadly fires in recent years. Road collisions are also common, attributed to poor maintenance and violations of traffic laws, and leading to thousands of road deaths a year.

articles.title: Hope for millions as cheaper HIV prevention jab reaches Africa
articles.snippet: Lenacapavir, administered as an injection twice a year, is nearly 100% effective at preventing HIV infection.
articles.full_text:
Hope for millions as cheaper HIV prevention jab reaches Africa
- Published
Uganda is set to receive its first supplies of a cheaper version of a ground-breaking injection to prevent HIV, raising hopes of expanding access to the drug across Africa, where the burden of the disease remains highest.
The first global shipment of the generic drug, known as lenacapavir, arrived in Zambia on Wednesday, with deliveries to Uganda expected in the coming days, the Global Fund has said.
The drug, administered as an injection twice a year, is nearly 100% effective at preventing HIV infection and is expected to cost just $40 (Â£30) per person annually.
Zimbabwe is due to receive supplies early next year, with several other countries expected to follow.
The arrival of the generic drug comes just a year after the original version, developed by US pharmaceutical giant Gilead Sciences, became available in sub-Saharan Africa.
The original version cost about about $28,000 annually in the US, putting it beyond the reach of many of those in developing countries.
Lenacapavir works by targeting the protective protein shell of HIV, disrupting the virus's ability to multiply and establish an infection in the body.
In a landmark clinical trial involving more than 5,000 adolescent girls and young women in Uganda and South Africa in 2024, none of those who received the injection contracted HIV.
Health experts say the injection offers a major advantage over existing HIV prevention pills, known as pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP), which must be taken every day and can carry social stigma.
The World Health Organization (WHO) recommended the drug for HIV prevention in July 2025.
The Global Fund described the arrival of the drug in Africa as a "major breakthrough" in the fight against HIV, saying cheaper supplies would help reach millions more people at risk of infection.
"These deliveries mark an unprecedented acceleration and expansion in access to a highly effective, quality-assured generic HIV prevention medicine in low- and middle-income settings," the group said in a statement on Wednesday.
More than 189,000 people across 10 countries have already received their first injection of lenacapavir, according to the Global Fund.
The organisation expects 24 countries to have received supplies by the end of this year and, working with the US government, plans to reach at least three million people by the end of 2028.
It is eventually expected to be available in 120 low- and middle-income countries.
Sub-Saharan Africa accounts for nearly two-thirds of people living with HIV globally, with adolescent girls and young women disproportionately affected.
South Africa has the world's largest HIV-positive population, with nearly eight million people living with the virus. It is among the countries expected to receive the cheaper injection.
Some 41 million people worldwide were living with HIV last year, while 570,000 died from HIV-related illnesses, according to the WHO.
The rollout comes amid concerns that sweeping cuts to US foreign aid under President Donald Trump's administration could undermine decades of progress in tackling HIV in Africa, where many countries rely heavily on international funding for prevention and treatment.
The UN aims to end Aids as a public health threat by 2030.

articles.title: Why are winter rains forcing Palestinians in Gaza to flee again?
articles.source: Al Jazeera – Breaking News, World News and Video from Al Jazeera
articles.snippet: Israeli restrictions on humanitarian aid, damaged buildings and flooded tents leave displaced Palestinians vulnerable.
articles.full_text:
Why are winter rains forcing Palestinians in Gaza to flee again?
Israeli restrictions on humanitarian aid, damaged buildings and flooded tents leave displaced Palestinians vulnerable.
When heavy rain swept through az-Zawayda in central Gaza in early November, water rushed into Jaber al-Kaseeh’s tent, soaking his family’s mattresses and spoiling their food.
Al-Kaseeh, who fled Beit Lahiya in northern Gaza, told Al Jazeera that his camp had flooded three or four times the previous winter. Those floods had already driven many of his neighbours away.

About 1.36 million Palestinians, 65 percent of Gaza’s population, are living in tents and makeshift shelters, according to the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA).
The storm that began on the evening of November 6 flooded about 70,000 tents within 12 hours, according to Gaza’s Government Media Office. Preliminary UN estimates suggest it affected about 226,000 people, including more than 5,000 households left sleeping without shelter. About 600 households were forced to move again.
The rain also killed people. On November 8, a sand embankment collapsed onto tents at a displacement camp south of Deir el-Balah, killing five people, including children. OCHA reported that an infant drowned during the same storm and a nine-month-old baby died of hypothermia on November 13.
The Union of Gaza Strip Municipalities warned on Wednesday that about 1,000 camps and other shelter sites could flood this winter. The councils say 200,000 worn-out tents need replacing and more than 2,000 damaged buildings are at risk of collapse.
As Gaza enters its fourth winter since Israel launched its genocidal war in October 2023, we look at how Israeli restrictions on humanitarian aid, damaged buildings and flooded tents leave displaced Palestinians at greater risk.
Why can’t Palestinians move somewhere safer?
Israeli restrictions keep Palestinians from reaching large parts of Gaza, which leaves them fewer options to move to safer areas, according to OCHA. On November 17, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) and the World Food Programme said Gaza’s population had been confined to less than 40 percent of the territory and that more than half of its 1,700 displacement sites were on flood-prone land.
The threat of further displacement persists. On Thursday, Israel Katz, the defence minister in Israel’s caretaker government, threatened a new offensive that would move one million Palestinians south if Hamas did not disarm. Writing on X, he called Hamas’s control over the remaining 30 percent of Gaza “an illusion”. He did not issue an evacuation order.
Damaged homes offer little refuge. About 82 percent of Gaza’s structures had been damaged or destroyed by mid-June, according to UN satellite analysis.
In Nuseirat, Nasser al-Hajj took his children to a neighbour’s home during the first November storm as debris fell from the ceiling of his flat, which an Israeli attack had damaged. “But where am I supposed to go? Rent is expensive, and a tent is not safe either,” he told Al Jazeera.
Why is Gaza so vulnerable to flooding?
Israel’s war has wrecked the drains and sewers that would normally carry rainwater away. In Gaza City, eight pumping stations and three main rainwater collection basins were out of service when the first storm hit, municipal spokesperson Hosni Muhanna said. Even under the best conditions, he said, the remaining network could handle no more than a fifth of the rainwater.
At Sheikh Radwan lagoon, one of the city’s main collection basins, the water rose by nearly 1.5 metres (five feet) during the storm, OCHA reported. Its pumping station is operating at less than 40 percent of its design capacity, the UN office added on Thursday.
In central Gaza, the councils are worried about water rising suddenly in Wadi Gaza and flooding al-Mughraqa and az-Zahra. Emergency services are overstretched: Gaza’s civil defence said it received 2,166 distress calls on November 7 but could send crews to only 218; most callers received advice by phone.
What are the health risks?
During the early November rains, the UN said crews used suction trucks to remove water mixed with sewage from 58 shelters. At the Patient’s Friends Benevolent Society Hospital in Gaza City, water flooded the basement that housed the children’s department, pharmacy and radiology services. Elsewhere, flooded roads kept patients and staff from reaching clinics.
Crowding poses a separate risk. Families in crowded tents have too little water to maintain basic hygiene, paediatrician Sharif Matar told Al Jazeera at Gaza City’s Rantisi Children’s Hospital.
The World Health Organization (WHO) recorded 692 suspected meningitis cases between October 1 and November 23, most of them among babies under a year old. Gaza’s Ministry of Health issued an epidemic alert on November 24 after recording 272 cases in October, compared with a usual monthly average of 30 to 50.
Why isn’t enough shelter aid reaching families?
On November 13, the UN’s humanitarian team said more than 150,000 tents bought by aid organisations and governments were waiting outside Gaza, most of them in Egypt’s El Arish. On Wednesday, the European Commission said tents were still waiting on trucks because Israel had not allowed them or the equipment needed to put them up to enter. Goods from Egypt are routed for inspection through the Karem Abu Salem crossing (called Kerem Shalom in Israel) rather than entering directly through Rafah. Israeli authorities also classify some shelter supplies as “dual-use”, which limits how much aid groups can bring in.
COGAT, the Israeli military body that coordinates aid, said on Monday that nearly 100,000 tents had entered Gaza under its winter programme. It said it had approved more than 67,000 tents and other winter supplies that had yet to be brought in. Inside Gaza, shelter agencies have fewer than 6,500 tents in stock, the Norwegian Refugee Council (NRC) said on Wednesday.
Restrictions and shortages have pushed up prices. Basic winter supplies for a family of six can cost more than $6,000 inside Gaza, compared with about $700 when aid agencies buy them abroad and bring them in, the NRC said. Donors have funded only 35 percent of the $283m needed for the minimum winter shelter response.
A tent crossing the border tells a family little about when help will reach its camp. In al-Mawasi, near Khan Younis, Fadi Wafi told the Palestinian news agency Wafa on Wednesday that his name had been put on a list of people affected by the last storm, but he had received no shelter supplies. His family of five had two mattresses and two blankets.
What can be done before the next storm?
Gaza’s Government Media Office warned on Tuesday that it expected another storm within days. Aid workers have cleared drains, reinforced shelters and put up flood barriers, but OCHA reported on November 20 that such work had been recorded at only 162 of the 356 flood-prone locations that teams were tracking.
On Monday, IOM said Israeli authorities had approved about 70,000 pieces of timber and more than 1,200 toolkits to build sturdier emergency shelters for about 1,200 families. COGAT also said it had approved pumps and generators and would allow partial repairs at the Sheikh Ijlin and Sheikh Radwan sewage facilities. It did not say the equipment had arrived. COGAT has said reconstruction equipment will enter only after Hamas has fully disarmed. Gaza’s municipalities are still asking for pumps, backup generators and fuel.
For Om Hani Hamouda, whose family has been displaced about 15 times, the question is what they can live in when it rains again. “We want these tents to be replaced with caravans,” she told Al Jazeera after her tent flooded in az-Zawayda. “Even a simple caravan would be better.”

Judge strikes down Trump’s latest restrictions on US birthright citizenship
After a Supreme Court ruling against it, the Trump administration had tried a narrower set of restrictions.
A United States federal judge has blocked an attempt by President Donald Trump’s administration to deny birthright citizenship to certain categories of US-born children whose parents it argued were not subject to US jurisdiction.
In a ruling issued on Wednesday, District Court Judge Christopher Cooper said those children were still under US jurisdiction and thus were guaranteed citizenship under the US Constitution.

“The president cannot carve out new exceptions to birthright citizenship for children born within the United States and subject to its laws,” Cooper said in the order.
Another court in Maryland had also blocked the same policy by the Trump administration in a September ruling, issuing a preliminary injunction at the time.
The new ruling is another blow to Trump’s campaign to end birthright citizenship for children whose parents were not American citizens or legal permanent residents at their birth.
The Trump administration has argued that the US Constitution’s 14th Amendment – which says all “persons born or naturalised in the United States, and subject to the jurisdiction thereof, are citizens of the United States” – was not meant to apply to parents who were not permanently living in the country.
The latest lawsuit was brought by several rights groups on behalf of children who would be affected by Trump’s executive orders in August that targeted birthright citizenship.
US Supreme Court precedent
The case was heard after the US Supreme Court struck down Trump’s initial order on birthright citizenship in June, ruling that the lawmakers who drafted the 14th Amendment knew how broad its language was and did not limit it in the way the president was trying to.
Trump, who had taken the rare step of personally attending arguments at the Supreme Court in that case, has said he is unhappy with the June ruling.
In it, the Supreme Court cited a previous case it had considered in 1898 brought by a US-born Chinese American who was being denied citizenship. Wong Kim Ark’s parents had left the US for their native China after he was born, and when Wong returned as an adult, he was denied entry with officials saying he was not considered a citizen.
Soon after the Supreme Court’s ruling, Trump tried to again restrict birthright citizenship with a new order taking aim at “birth tourism”, in which women travel to the US to give birth so their children can obtain automatic citizenship. The order also targeted children whose parents work for foreign governments or international organizations but lack diplomatic immunity and those who have a parent who is classified as an “alien enemy”.
The president “needs to accept that birthright citizenship is the law of the land”, said Cody Wofsy, a lawyer with the American Civil Liberties Union, one of the groups representing plaintiffs in the latest case. “The Supreme Court has twice rejected efforts to gut birthright citizenship, in 1898 and again earlier this year. Third time is not the charm.”
White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said in a statement that the court’s decision was “just another ruling from an activist judge” and Trump’s order had been “consistent with the holdings and analysis set forth by the Supreme Court”.
In a study last year, the Migration Policy Institute estimated that about 255,000 babies a year who were born to parents who were unauthorised immigrants or on temporary visas and thus subject to Trump’s initial executive order would be denied citizenship if the Supreme Court had upheld that policy.
Roots in the US Civil War era
The 14th Amendment, ratified in 1868 after the US Civil War, automatically made those born to previously enslaved people citizens of the country. Its broad language, though, also extended to others born in the country, an interpretation US courts have said was in line with English traditions preceding the founding of the United States.
Indigenous people were seen as an exception to that provision because they enjoyed some legal autonomy, and it was not until 1924 that the US Congress passed a law granting them citizenship.
Since taking office, Trump has set out a broad agenda to restrict immigration, restricting visas and political asylum for much of the world and directing federal law enforcement agencies to institute a national crackdown on allegedly undocumented immigrants.
Along with trying to restrict who is granted birthright citizenship, the Trump administration has also stepped up lawsuits to strip already naturalised people of their status if they committed major crimes and concealed that history from authorities.

articles.title: Psychiatric care under scrutiny after abuse scandals in Croatia and Bosnia

Psychiatric care under scrutiny after abuse scandals in Croatia and Bosnia
Persistent failures in psychiatric care have been exposed, including staff shortages, inadequate training and weak oversight.
Thousands gathered in Zagreb’s Ban Josip Jelacic Square on Saturday, carrying white pillows marked with bloody handprints.
The symbolic protest was held in memory of 32-year-old Kristian Josip Peris, who died at the Sveti Ivan Psychiatric Clinic in the Croatian capital after medical staff allegedly tried to restrain him by placing a pillow over his face, according to publicly released security camera footage.
Recommended Stories

- list 2 of 4EU tells TikTok to fix ‘harmful’ For You feed, threatens fines
- list 3 of 4Traumas of Sudan war lead to wave of drug addiction

Several days later, footage from the psychiatric ward of a public hospital in the city of Zenica, in neighbouring Bosnia and Herzegovina, sparked public outrage. The video showed medical staff physically assaulting a patient.
The two cases in neighbouring countries led to the arrest of at least 13 healthcare workers, the resignations of the heads of the psychiatric institutions involved, and a wave of public anger.
But they also raised a broader question: What happens behind the closed doors of institutions meant to protect some of society’s most vulnerable people?
These are not the first cases to have shocked the region.
Bosnia and Herzegovina still remembers the Pazaric institutional abuse scandal, involving a small settlement located about 30km (18.6 miles) from the capital, Sarajevo, where residents of a state institution for children and young people with additional needs were tied to radiators and subjected to physical abuse.
Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina, once part of the same country, Yugoslavia, have spent the past three decades trying to bring their healthcare systems and societies closer to European standards.
Croatia joined the European Union in 2013, while Bosnia and Herzegovina is forging its own path towards membership.
Unlike in some Western countries, where private healthcare providers play a significant role in mental health services, psychiatric inpatient care in Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina and Serbia is predominantly provided through public healthcare institutions.
Although private providers also operate in the region, public institutions remain central to the provision of specialised psychiatric hospital care.
This makes the role of public authorities particularly important, not only in ensuring access to treatment but also in supervising institutions, maintaining adequate staffing levels and protecting patients’ rights.
‘Problem lies in consistently following those protocols’
Edin Bjelosevic, a neuropsychiatrist and university professor from Zenica, said the legal frameworks in countries that emerged from the breakup of Yugoslavia largely reflect contemporary standards for treating people with mental health conditions.
“The problem lies in consistently following those protocols, rather than in access to modern treatments and procedures,” Bjelosevic told Al Jazeera.
According to Eurostat, the EU’s statistical office, about 96,000 psychiatrists were working across 25 member countries in 2024. Germany had the highest number relative to its population, with 29 psychiatrists per 100,000 people. Croatia recorded 19.1, above the European average, while Serbia had 12.4 psychiatrists per 100,000 people.
Bosnia and Herzegovina, according to World Health Organization (WHO) data from 2020, had just 9.48 psychiatrists per 100,000 people. More recent comparable figures for the country are not available.
Differences are also evident in the number of psychiatric hospital beds. Croatia had 93 beds per 100,000 people, compared with the European average of 71. Serbia recorded 82, while Bosnia and Herzegovina, with 40 beds per 100,000 people, was significantly below the average.
Eurostat and WHO figures may differ from data published by national statistical agencies.
However, the number of psychiatrists and hospital beds alone does not provide a complete picture of the quality of care, patient safety or the working conditions of healthcare professionals.
Staff shortages increase risks
In its 2024-2025 report, Croatia’s Ombudswoman called on the Ministry of Health to improve the functioning of psychiatric institutions. Among the recommendations was better training for medical staff in the use of coercive measures involving people with mental health conditions.
Coercive measures are used in psychiatric institutions around the world. They involve temporarily restricting a patient’s freedom of movement to prevent an immediate risk of harm to themselves or others. However, they are not intended as a routine means of controlling patients, but as a last resort when other approaches have failed.
Following Peris’s death, Croatia’s Ministry of Health identified shortcomings at the clinic, ordering five corrective measures.
The inspection found faults in staff training and staffing levels, alongside problems with the supervision of patients subjected to coercive measures, medical record-keeping and reporting procedures following the patient’s death.
Staffing levels did not meet the required standards, with a shortage of one physiotherapist and one nursing assistant. The ministry also found faults in the scope and quality of staff training on managing patients in crisis situations.
Health Minister Irena Hrstic said four of the five corrective measures were to take effect immediately, while the clinic was given 60 days to bring its staffing levels into line with the required standards.
The findings highlighted concerns that go beyond the conduct of individual healthcare workers, raising questions about staffing, training and institutional oversight in psychiatric care.
Abdulah Kucukalic, a neuropsychiatrist from Sarajevo, said psychiatric institutions across the region share a common problem: a shortage of non-medical personnel specifically trained to deal safely with patients experiencing acute psychiatric crises.
“I think the legislation is in line with, or very close to, international standards. Our doctors are also frequently cited in international professional circles. But our psychiatric institutions lack non-medical staff trained to manage patients safely,” Kucukalic told Al Jazeera.
He warned that situations are particularly risky when patients in severe acute conditions arrive at hospitals in the late afternoon or at night, when staffing levels are significantly lower.
“My experience is that patients in acute conditions arrive in the afternoon or at night, in extremely serious states. At that point, you may have just one doctor and two healthcare workers in the hospital. They are not in a position to manage such a patient safely,” Kucukalic said.
The cases in Zagreb and Zenica illustrate how thin the line can be between providing care and putting at risk the very people who need protection most.

President says it was a deliberate decision to release ‘fake’ growth numbers before US midterm elections.
United States President Donald Trump has accused his Department of Commerce of purposely issuing incorrect economic growth figures before the midterm elections and says he wants to launch an investigation.
Trump made his comments on Thursday when offices and stock markets were closed for the Thanksgiving holiday.

The US Commerce Department’s Bureau of Economic Analysis on Wednesday revised third-quarter annualised growth up to 4.3 percent from the advance estimate of 3.4 percent it announced on October 29. Trump’s Republican Party suffered heavy losses in the November 3 elections.
“It was just revealed that the REAL Numbers on the Economy, published before the Election, were FAKE,” Trump said in a Truth Social post without providing evidence for the accusation.
“Why wasn’t the correct number issued before the Election? I am asking for an immediate investigation of this situation. This is not a small error, this is a massive, and purposeful, error,” he said.
Trump has repeatedly sought to undermine trust in economic data that fail to match his claims of a historic boom, a pattern that threatens the credibility of figures needed by businesses, financial markets and consumers when making investments.
The Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) routinely updates its economic data to improve their accuracy. Gross domestic product (GDP) figures, monthly jobs reports and other data are regularly revised. Those updates occur on a prescheduled basis without regard to the political calendar.
The BEA did not immediately respond to a request for comment. It has previously said GDP estimates can differ from the final numbers because advance estimates for quarterly growth lack complete source data on inventories, trade and consumer spending on services.
A May article coauthored by BEA Director Vipin Arora found that for GDP, the estimates released 90 days after initial estimates typically differed by 0.52 percentage points throughout this century.
“That is, over these 25 years, more complete source data expanded or contracted BEA’s estimates of real GDP growth on average by about half a percentage point per quarter,” wrote Arora and coauthor Rebecca Pocase.
Last year, Trump fired a top Department of Labor official after a weak jobs report, accusing her without evidence of manipulating the figures, a move that added to already growing concerns about the quality of economic data published by the federal government.

Guinea-Bissau military leaders delay presidential election until 2028
Military leaders say presidential and legislative poll scheduled for December 6 will now take place in November 2028.
Guinea-Bissau’s military leaders have delayed next month’s presidential and legislative election by two years, pushing back a vote that was meant to return the country to civilian rule.
A decree issued on Thursday by the transitional president, Major-General Horta Inta-a, said the elections initially scheduled for December 6 would instead take place in November 2028.

The decree said there was “an insufficiency of the technical, material and financial conditions” necessary to hold the vote.
The army seized power in the West African country last November, disrupting a presidential vote and overthrowing the incumbent, Umaro Sissoco Embalo, who was seeking a new term.
The coup inaugurated former army chief of staff Inta-a as head of the military government, tasked with overseeing a one-year transition period.

articles.title: Estimates of Russians killed in Ukraine surpass all combined US war deaths since WWI
articles.snippet: More than 700,000 Russian soldiers have been killed in the war in Ukraine since Russia launched its full-scale war against the nation nearly five years ago.
articles.full_text:
More than 700,000 Russian soldiers have been killed in the war in Ukraine since Russia launched its full-scale war against the nation nearly five years ago, according to an updated estimate released on Monday.
Based on analysis of leaked official data by Belarusian and Ukrainian hackers from Russia’s statistical bureau, Rosstat, two Russian opposition outlets, Mediazona and Meduza, have confirmed that, accounting for time lags and troops reported missing in action, Russian fatalities jumped from 490,000 at the end of September to more than 720,000 since the start of the conflict in February 2022.
That number, CNN reports, equates to roughly one death every four minutes. The estimate does not include the number of soldiers wounded.
“We are confident that this data is authentic: it is verified against the list of names of the deceased (including records not yet published), the Register of Inheritance Cases, other leaked records from civil registry offices, the texts of court decisions from open sources, and previously published data from Rosstat itself,” Meduza reported.
The Kremlin has not officially updated its death toll in Ukraine since the early start of the war, when then-Defense Minister Sergei Shoigu acknowledged that it stood at nearly 6,000. This has left many Russian civilians with perhaps little understanding of the full breadth of the conflict as President Vladimir Putin continues to suppress critical information regarding the war at home.
This grim assessment is particularly stark when placed next to U.S. military casualties. If accurate, the number of Russians dead in Ukraine has surpassed all combined U.S. military deaths since World War I.
According to official DoD numbers — exact death counts vary, with historians often clashing over official counts for years, even decades — the U.S. suffered 116,516 total military deaths in WWI; 405,399 military deaths in WWII; 36,574 military deaths during the Korean War; 58,220 during the Vietnam War; 382 in the Persian Gulf War; 2,459 in Afghanistan; 4,493 in Iraq; and 362 military deaths from conflicts in Grenada, Panama, Somalia and Beirut.
The total, 624,547, spanning over 100 years, still falls far below that of Russia in the past five.
While 700,000 lives lost is staggering, it still pales when compared to Soviet dead after Nazi Germany launched Operation Barbarossa in June 1941. During four years of war, it is estimated that 8.8 million to 10.7 million Soviet soldiers were killed. Combined with civilian deaths, that estimate hovers around the grim figure of 24 million Soviet deaths.

articles.title: US Air Force buys final KC-46 lot under Boeing’s original tanker deal
articles.snippet: The Pentagon announced a $2.82 billion Boeing contract for 15 more KC-46A Pegasus tankers, the final production lot under the program's original 2011 contract.
articles.full_text:
The Pentagon on Tuesday announced a $2.82 billion Boeing contract for 15 more KC-46A Pegasus tankers, the final production lot under the program’s original 2011 contract.
The deal comes in about $350 million above the previous 15-tanker lot, which the Air Force bought for $2.47 billion a year ago. The earlier lot is expected to be complete by mid-2029 and the new lot by mid-2030, according to the Pentagon.
The Air Force has received 116 KC-46As so far, and 203 are on contract or in service worldwide, Boeing said. Japan and Israel also fly the tanker.
“We’re grateful for the trust the U.S. Air Force continues to place in our team,” Jake Kwasnik, KC-46 program vice president, said in Boeing’s release. “The KC-46 plays an important role in enabling military operations around the world, and we look forward to building on that partnership while staying focused on delivering on our commitments to support the warfighter.”
Tuesday’s award is the last of 13 production lots priced into the original contract, Boeing’s filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission show.
After that, the Air Force plans to buy up to 75 more KC-46As from Boeing through a program called Tanker Production Extension, according to an April contracting notice. The service wants 263 KC-46As for itself, which it says will fully replace its KC-135s, built in the 1950s and early 1960s.
Air Force Vice Chief of Staff Gen. John Lamontagne said the 75-jet buy depends on Boeing fixing some of the tanker’s problems, Reuters reported. He didn’t specifically identify the problems, but the best-known KC-46A issues involve the refueling boom and the Remote Vision System, or RVS, the cameras boom operators use to guide it.
“We are working through a couple of issues with the contractor, and we are not going to get a new contract for another 75 KC-46s until we work through some of those deficiencies,” Lamontagne told a Senate Armed Services subcommittee March 4. He said a decision was likely two years away.
Boeing said in June it had completed the first phase of flight testing on a redesigned RVS 2.0. The Air Force has projected fielding the upgraded system in summer 2027, three years later than originally planned.
The KC-46 program has been costly for Boeing. It built the tanker under a firm-fixed-price contract, which leaves the company to cover cost overruns, and has recorded more than $7 billion in losses, including $565 million late last year that Boeing blamed on higher production costs.
The service has said the main issues keeping KC-46s from being ready to fly are the reliability of the aerial refueling system and parts shortages. In May, the Air Force and Boeing agreed on a plan that, along with funding in the fiscal 2027 budget request, is expected to increase KC-46 availability by more than 20% by 2030.

articles.title: Air Force issues Boeing $2.8 billion for more KC-46s
articles.snippet: The award brings the total number of air refuelers under contract to 203, and is the final production batch for the US Air Force under the program’s original fixed-price contract.
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON — The US Air Force has awarded Boeing $2.8 billion to build a new batch of KC-46 Pegasus air refuelers, the Pentagon announced.
The award for the aircraft’s 13th production lot covers 15 aircraft, with work expected to wrap up by the end of June 2030, according to the Defense Department contract notice, published Tuesday. The aircraft is manufactured by Boeing at the company’s facilities in Seattle, Wash.
“We’re grateful for the trust the U.S. Air Force continues to place in our team,” Jake Kwasnik, Boeing’s vice president for the KC-46 program, said in a company press release. “The KC-46 plays an important role in enabling military operations around the world, and we look forward to building on that partnership while staying focused on delivering on our commitments to support the warfighter.”
The Tuesday award brings the total number of refuelers under contract to 203, inclusive of foreign sales, according to Boeing. The company says it has so far delivered 116 Pegasus aircraft to the Air Force, as well as six to Japan and two to Israel. And other customers could be on the way, after the US in August cleared a KC-46 sale for Qatar.
The KC-46 is based on Boeing’s 767 commercial jet and is the US’s newest air refueler, which officials are buying to gradually recapitalize a fleet of aging KC-135 Stratotanker aircraft. In addition to gassing up other jets, the Pegasus can move cargo and people similar to other large mobility aircraft.
The Lot 13 award is the final under the program’s original fixed-price contract that kicked off in 2011, where developmental challenges and production woes have driven billions of dollars in losses for Boeing. The Air Force intends to continue the tanker’s production run under a new “extension” program and order up to 75 additional aircraft, which would commence with Lot 14, the service indicated in a previously published document. However, officials have said that future aircraft would come with price jumps.
Air Force officials have also pledged not to move forward with the extension plan unless the jet’s lingering top issues, known as category 1 deficiencies, are resolved. A key planned upgrade will address the aircraft’s troubled vision system that operators use to guide a refueling boom to receiving aircraft. The service expects to field that new remote vision system, dubbed RVS 2.0, beginning in early 2028.
The Air Force is buying more KC-46s as the service evaluates options for a follow-on tanking solution. The service is now launching a new round of analysis for its refueling plans, with an emphasis on enhancing existing aircraft, according to Aviation Week.
But some believe the Air Force needs a fresh approach for its tanker fleet. A recent report by the Hudson Institute recommended that officials should buy newly designed air refuelers — in this case, a blended-wing body aircraft — to provide greater range and fuel offload. The report’s authors argue that this new aircraft would be better suited for conflict with China.

articles.title: Japan to use Indian ranges for long-range missile training under new pact
articles.snippet: Japanese officials visited India in October to assess whether its missile ranges could accommodate training with anti-ship missiles and smaller attack drones.
articles.full_text:
NEW DELHI — India will allow Japanese troops to conduct live-fire missile training at its firing ranges for the first time as Tokyo looks overseas for facilities to test its long-range missile capabilities including surface-to-ship missiles.
The signing of a Letter of Intent (LOI) regarding the use of the Indian ranges was announced on Nov. 19, following a meeting between the two countries’ foreign and defense ministers in Tokyo.
The move marks a significant step in deepening defense cooperation between the two Asian countries.
Japanese officials visited India in October to assess whether its missile ranges could accommodate training with anti-ship missiles and smaller attack drones.
Chief of Staff of the Japan Ground Self-Defense Force Masayoshi Arai told reporters in Tokyo last month that the visit’s aim was to determine how to conduct training that makes full use of the roughly 1,000-kilometer range of Japan’s Type-25 surface-to-ship missile, which he described as “a major challenge.”
Limited space in the island country for long-range live-fire exercises has prompted officials to look for training options overseas. Access to Indian ranges could help overcome that limitation.
To bolster its military strength amid growing concerns over China’s military activity in the region, Japan began deploying long-range missiles on the southern island of Kyushu this year. The deployment is part of Japan’s effort to strengthen its deterrence and stand-off defense capabilities as it makes a significant shift in its post-World War II security posture.
A joint statement by the two countries after last week’s meeting welcomed the signing of the Letter of Intent, “whereby Japan Self-Defense Forces would, for the first time, conduct live-fire training etc., including those involving surface-to-ship missiles, at firing ranges in India.”
Japanese Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi said the arrangement was significant not only for expanding the scope of training for Japanese forces but also as a demonstration of a new phase in Japan-India cooperation.
The meeting between the Indian and Japanese defense ministers – their third in the last four months — also focused on enhancing military and arms industry cooperation between the two countries.
They agreed to accelerate negotiations toward finalizing their first-ever defense technology cooperation initiative under which India and Japan are jointly developing and manufacturing advanced integrated communication antenna systems for Indian Navy warships.
Developed for the Japanese navy, the Unified Complex Radio Antenna (UNICORN) system helps reduce the radar signature of naval vessels. Under the proposed agreement, a state run Indian company will collaborate with Japanese defense firms to co-produce the advanced mast for future Indian navy warships.
New Delhi has been seeking greater Japanese involvement in its defense industry and access to advanced technology as part of its efforts to strengthen domestic manufacturing.
After the talks in Tokyo, Indian Defense Minister Rajnath Singh said potential areas for collaboration between the two countries include naval shipbuilding, unmanned and autonomous systems and advanced defense technologies.
Amid their deepening defense cooperation, Japan deployed its fighter jets in India for the first time in September during a bilateral air exercise held in the Indian city of Jodhpur. Tokyo sent F-2A fighter aircraft for the exercise, known as Veer Guardian 2026.
At the recent meeting, both sides agreed to incorporate unmanned systems and increase the complexity of future exercises.

articles.title: Buried in Italy’s budget, officials see Rome meeting NATO spending target
articles.snippet: The numbers cannot be found in this year’s Italian defense budget, but the country has achieved a promised spending total on defense and domestic security equal to 2.8% of GDP in 2026, officials have claimed.
articles.full_text:
ROME — The numbers cannot be found in this year’s Italian defense budget, but the country has achieved a promised spending total on defense and domestic security equal to 2.8% of GDP in 2026, officials have claimed.
That means Italy has fulfilled a promise made at the July NATO summit to hit the 2.8% target as Rome tries to reach the alliance’s 5% objective by 2035, under pressure from U.S. President Trump.
The 5% ambition set down by NATO is split between 3.5% on core defense spending and 1.5% on domestic security spending. Italian officials told Defense News Rome’s spending in the first category hit 2.1% in 2026 and 0.7% in the second category this year, combining for the 2.8% total.
Italy’s 2026 budget, which was issued months late last week, does not clearly state this, and overall patience is required to understand what Italy is spending on each category.
Analysis of the budget starts with pure defense spending, meaning investment, personnel and maintenance and operations cash for the Italian Army, Air Force and Navy, listed as “Funzione Difesa.”
Unlike in previous years, no number is given, but it can be extrapolated from other figures, giving €23.6 billion ($25.8 billion), up from €22.49 billion last year, a €1.1 billion jump.
Within that spend is the key cash for investment or procurement, which is also not specified but can be calculated, by referring to other figures, as €9.33 billion out of the defense ministry’s coffers.
Add in top-funding from Italy’s Enterprise ministry for procurement and the total rises over €12 billion according to a graph which corresponds to the €12.77 billion reached by totaling the amounts listed for each procurement program.
The next total listed is the “Ordinary” defense budget, which adds in domestic spending on Italy’s paramilitary Carabinieri police and other smaller expenses.
That total stands at €32.4 billion in 2026, up 3.6 percent on last year’s €31.3 billion, with spending predicted to rise next year to €32.7 billion.
The next item is the “Integrated” defense budget, which adds all Enterprise Ministry spending, funding from Italy’s finance ministry for overseas military missions and cash from the European Union used for cyber defense.
That total is €36.79 billion, up from €35.49 billion last year.
The complicated calculation does not end there. Next up is the “NATO” budget, which adds in other spending which NATO counts as defense spending.
In the document, the extras are listed as, “Pension spending” and “Spending by other ministries that contribute to national defense.”
The new total is €48.31 billion, which is equal to 2.1% of GDP, up from 2% in 2025.
What the document does not reveal is the domestic security spending Italy then adds on top of that to reach its total figure of 2.8 percent of GDP, as declared at the NATO summit.
Government sources said the remaining cash, equivalent to 0.7% of GDP, is handled outside the defense budget.
Defense News calculated the spending is equal to about €16.1 billion.
The sources, who spoke on condition of anonymity said the spending covers various activities including: frontier control, combatting terrorism, protecting energy infrastructure and crisis preparation.

articles.title: Czech jet engine maker eyes growing role as US supplier in drones, missiles
articles.snippet: Czech jet engine producer PBS Aerospace aims to expand its manufacturing capacity in the United States, targeting at least a twofold increase in its production capacity there.
articles.full_text:
WARSAW, Poland — Czech jet engine producer PBS Aerospace aims to expand its manufacturing capacity in the United States, targeting at least a twofold increase in its production capacity there, according to senior company representatives.
Jan Havránek, PBS Aerospace’s chief government relations and strategy officer, told Defense News that is because the business is booming due to a rising demand for compact propulsion systems used in drones and cruise missiles.
“Everybody wants to build drones and missiles that are fast, fly far, and they want to have them now. That puts scale and quality at the center of the conversation,” Havránek said. “Global conflicts, including the war in Ukraine, have made clear how important it is for the United States to have a reliable domestic supply of these engines, and the market is moving quickly.”
While continuing to produce engines at its factory in Velká Bíteš, in the Czech Republic, PBS Aerospace expanded its American presence in September 2025 with the launch of a plant in Roswell, Georgia. The manufacturing facility was opened as part of a $20 million investment.
“We’re building engines in America, for America,” Havránek said. “Our Georgia facility serves the U.S. market first and foremost, with the U.S. government as our end customer. We supply engines to prime contractors that deliver systems to the Department of War, and we’re proud to help strengthen the U.S. defense industrial base and bring critical manufacturing back onshore.”
In the U.S., the group’s partners include Lockheed Martin and Pratt & Whitney.
To meet rising demand, PBS Aerospace plans to increase its Roswell facility’s annual output to between 10,000 and 20,000 engines over the next three years.
“For next year, we’re looking at up to 5,000 engines to be produced in America,” he said.
With the manufacturing ramp-up in mind, PBS Aerospace is planning to allocate around $100 million to boost its capacity in Roswell, according to Havránek.
Some of the company’s most sought-after products include the TJ40-G1, a compact jet engine that weighs 3.4 kg (7.5 pounds) and delivers up to 425 N of thrust, as indicated by data from the manufacturer.

articles.title: Ford in talks with the Pentagon to supply military vehicles
articles.snippet: Ford said on Tuesday it has held talks with the Pentagon about supplying military vehicles and other defense products to the U.S. military.
articles.full_text:
Ford said on Tuesday it has held talks with the Pentagon about supplying military vehicles and other defense products to the U.S. military, as legacy automakers seek a share of fast-rising defense spending amid tough competition in the auto sector.
A Ford spokesperson said the discussions were focused on supplying highly capable military vehicles and working with U.S.-based space systems contractor Revolution Space to build advanced satellites. Ford had announced on Monday a minority investment in Revolution Space.
The Wall Street Journal first reported earlier in the day that the Pentagon was in talks with General Motors, Ford and other manufacturers to help mass-produce military drones by supplying parts including actuators, engines, sensors and lidar to drone companies.
“The Department of War is actively partnering with domestic manufacturers, suppliers, and emerging tech firms to build a resilient, high-capacity industrial base that accelerates the production, deployment, and long-term sustainment of next-generation unmanned and autonomous systems,” a Pentagon official told Reuters.
Detroit’s automakers have a long history of turning mass production capabilities toward military needs, having converted factories during World War II to build tanks, jet engines and trucks.
According to the Journal’s report, GM is weighing whether to manufacture drone motors, while U.S. defense officials have met with executives at Canadian auto parts maker Magna International and other manufacturing firms, some outside the auto industry.
GM has been most interested in getting involved with military projects at the request of high-ranking defense officials, the Journal said, adding that the automaker was in talks with RTX and L3Harris on a similar deal.
GM declined to comment on the report, but said in an emailed statement that its Defense unit has extensive capabilities and scale, and that it has “demonstrated our commitment to reinforce the U.S. defense-industrial base and help address critical needs.”
Magna said it had nothing to add with regard to the report.

articles.title: NATO sees no Russian naval buildup in the Med after strike near Libya, but analysts warn of wider risks
articles.snippet: Experts say Ukraine’s strike could have consequences far beyond Libya, raising the risk of Russian retaliation and heightened tensions along NATO’s southern flank.
articles.full_text:
MILAN — While NATO does not anticipate a Russian naval buildup in the Mediterranean after a recent Ukrainian drone strike near Libya, the operation has raised concerns about the risk of drawing the North African country deeper into the war and threatening the alliance’s southern flank.
Ukraine used unmanned vessels to strike two Russian ships near the Libyan port of Benghazi along the Mediterranean coast on Sunday, sinking a warship and damaging a cargo vessel, according to the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU). Despite questions about the potential for a wider response from Moscow, NATO “is not expecting a surge or redeployment of further Russian assets in the Mediterranean,” an alliance official told Breaking Defense.
That is largely because the Russian surface fleet “is having serious war-generation issues,” according to the NATO official, who spoke on condition of anonymity.
The alliance is more concerned about the conflict spilling over into other areas and the potential for attacks on commercial shipping, both in the Mediterranean and elsewhere, the official said. Such attacks, they added, have already been seen in the Black Sea, where Russia has targeted “innocent merchant shipping.”
NATO routinely evaluates its force posture and readiness in the [Mediterranean] region, the official added. They noted that on any given day, the average “ratio of NATO deployed assets to those of Russia is 3:1” — meaning that for every one Russian surface ship, there are three allied surface ships underway. That imbalance is even greater in the Mediterranean, where the alliance’s deployed assets outnumber Russia’s by roughly 5-6 to 1, the official added.
Although NATO does not anticipate an immediate shift in the Russian naval presence, questions remain about how Kyiv conducted the operation and what it could mean for the region.
Earlier this year, the Associated Press reported that Libyan officials said Ukrainian forces, most of them drone specialists, had been operating from military facilities in western Libya. The officials, who spoke to the AP on condition of anonymity, identified an air base in Misrata as the main site, along with facilities in Tripoli and the coastal town of Zawiya.
Libyan officials briefed on Sunday’s attack also told the AP that the Russian corvette was struck at the Benghazi Naval Base, claiming that at least four drones were intercepted while two hit the vessel.
The Ukrainian SBU, meanwhile, said the seven naval drones were delivered to a designated location and launched into the water from a “mothership” near the target. The agency did not identify the vessel or specify where the drones were launched, leaving questions about whether the operation originated from Libyan territory.
Deep divisions remain across the North African country following the 2011 overthrow of the Muammar Gaddafi regime and the subsequent civil wars that erupted. The western part of Libya, largely centered around Tripoli, is controlled by the UN-recognized Government of National Unity (GNU), formed in 2021 and led by Prime Minister Abdul Hamid Dbeibeh.
Meanwhile, eastern Libya is controlled by rival authorities aligned with military commander Khalifa Haftar and his Libyan National Army (LNA). The area shares close ties to Moscow, as authorities have allowed Russian naval vessels to use the port of Tobruk as a resupply and refueling hub.
According to Arturo Varvelli, head of the Rome office and senior policy fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations, it remains unclear whether Ukraine launched its attack from western Libya, as the claim has not yet been independently verified, even by Moscow. However, he warned that the operation could have serious ripple effects for the region and possibly draw the war in Ukraine closer to NATO’s southern flank.
“The United Nations’ mission has already called for an independent investigation, warning against the risk of dragging Libya into foreign conflicts,” Varvalli told Breaking Defense. “This is precisely the greatest strategic danger: that Libya could turn into yet another theater of the war between Russia and Ukraine, just a few hundred kilometers from Italy.”
He referred to statements by Aydar Aganin, Moscow’s ambassador to Libya, who was quoted by Russian state media outlet RT as saying the attack “will not go unanswered” and that Moscow is weighing its options. While Varvelli assesses that an armed retaliation against western Libya is unlikely in the immediate future, an asymmetric response is more probable.
“Eastern authorities have stated that Libya ‘reserves the right to respond by all necessary means’; however, I believe a direct kinetic response against western Libya is unlikely in the short term, as the costs for both sides would be extremely high,” he said.
One potential complication for Moscow is the presence of foreign military personnel in Misrata, where Ukraine’s main base is reportedly located at the Air Force Academy. The coastal city in northwestern Libya is aligned with the UN-backed GNU, and the facility is reportedly shared with Turkish and Italian forces, US Africa Command (AFRICOM) and a British intelligence center.
“An attack by Russia or the Libyan National Army [governed by Haftar] on Misrata would risk striking Turkish, Italian or US personnel present in the area,” Varvelli said. “Asymmetric responses are more likely. … Consequently, any retaliation might more simply be directed against Kyiv.”
Italy has maintained a military presence in the western part of the country since 2018 through its Bilateral Mission of Assistance and Support in Libya (MIASIT).
Vincenzo Camporini, Italy’s former chief of defense general staff, also raised concerns about potential Russian retaliation. In an interview published Monday by Italian media Agenzia Nova, Camporini warned that if Moscow retaliated against western Libya — possibly by encouraging LNA forces to act — it could risk reigniting a civil war inside the country, only this time with greater direct involvement from Russia and Turkey.
On Tuesday, the GNU’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation stated that Libya’s territory would not be used as a staging ground for attacks and referred to the strike in Benghazi as highlighting “the danger of hosting foreign forces that operate outside the authority of the state.”
Kyiv has also pushed back against suggestions that it is expanding the war beyond Ukraine. Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha posted on his Telegram channel on Tuesday that “Ukraine is not ‘dragging’ anyone into the war or ‘transferring’ the war anywhere.”

articles.title: Israel increases defense budget by $5 billion as concerns continue over future funding
articles.snippet: Israel has scrambled several times this year to increase its defense spending, at the cost of other priorities.
articles.full_text:
JERUSALEM — Israel’s Joint Committee on the Defense Budget has approved a $5 billion increase to Israel’s defense budget, despite the ongoing uncertainty about who will be prime minister in the wake of the country’s Oct. 27 elections, and budget challenges nationwide.
Israel Katz, the country’s defense minister, said that he welcomed the decision by the committee “to approve an addition of approximately NIS 17.3 billion to the 2026 defense budget, as part of the initiative I led to strengthen the IDF’s capabilities and build up its forces for the coming years.”
He added that the approval will enable Israel to “advance plans for blue-and-white self-reliance in long-term procurement in space, attack helicopters, air defense, and other classified areas.”
The term “blue and white,” the colors of the Israeli flag, refers to an effort by Israel’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to make Israel more independent in defense production by investing heavily in local companies and products.
However, the spending increase will only do so much to shore up defense plans in the wake of budget shortfalls that will stretch into 2027.
In March 2026, Israel approved a record defense budget of $45 billion, but it has continued to receive supplemental spending, including a transfer in August of around $300 million, a $5 billion increase in September and an October deal to fund Apache helicopter purchases. It would appear that Tuesday’s committee decision would bring the defense budget to around $55 billion. These increases were funded by moving money from one part of the approved budget, like from the Ministries of Transport, National Security and Education, among others, to the defense ministry.
At the time, Israeli Ministry of Defense Director General Amir Baram said the Apache deal was made possible due to “creative solutions we developed together with our American partners,” without elaborating on what that means. He did note that the ministry was working to sign more agreements for unnamed “platforms, munitions, interceptors, and more. This is to ensure immediate readiness for any scenario, alongside the implementation of the decade-long force buildup plan, as part of the IMOD’s strategy in the face of emerging challenges.”
In addition, Israel appears to be in debt to its own state-run defense giants, Israel Aerospace Industries and Rafael Advanced Defense Systems.
On Nov. 12, IAI announced its third quarter financial results. In its statement it noted that “as of September 30, 2026, the Israeli Ministry of Defense’s outstanding debt to Israel Aerospace Industries amounts to billions of shekels and is reflected in the company’s financial results. Israel Aerospace Industries calls on the Ministry of Defense and the Ministry of Finance to urgently reach an agreement to settle this outstanding debt.”
Rafael has not released a statement about the debt issue, although Israel’s Calcalist publication said in October that the debt is around $2.3 billion to Rafael and around $2 billion to IAI.
The budget challenges will seemingly continue into the new year, especially following the announced end of US military aid. It is unclear, however, when or how that will go into effect.
In addition, the new Knesset in Israel is now led by the opposition, even though the opposition has not been able to form a new government. If this situation continues it will also affect the budget discussion in 2027.
“We will continue to act decisively to ensure Israel’s military superiority and give the IDF the tools it needs to protect our citizens and prevail in every arena,” Katz said.
